## Oct 23 Results: Maximum Accuracy, Minimum Sample

In the perpetual tension between sample size and outcome, yesterday provided the least statistically meaningful perfect record possible: 1-0. The model projected Milwaukee at 55% against Tampa Bay, and variance cooperated. Let's be clear—a single correct prediction tells us virtually nothing about model skill, but it does keep our cumulative win rate climbing. We'll take the green check mark while acknowledging the underlying statistical reality.

## The 55% Win Probability Zone

Yesterday's projection fell into what I call the "statistical honesty zone"—close enough to 50% that we're essentially admitting the game could go either way, but with enough lean to identify marginal value. A 55% projection converting to a win is exactly what should happen 55% of the time over infinite trials. One instance? Noise. But directionally correct noise is always preferable.

## Oct 24 Preview: Same Teams, Different Variance Draw

The baseball gods have granted us an immediate rematch: Rays at Brewers, take two. But the underlying probabilities have shifted to a perfect coin flip at 50%. This is the model's way of saying the expected value differential has evaporated. The pitching matchup—Drew Rasmussen against Logan Henderson—presents more uncertainty than yesterday's arms.

## Pitcher Matchup Analysis: Rasmussen vs Henderson

Drew Rasmussen brings a track record of volatility—high strikeout upside paired with occasional command lapses. Logan Henderson profiles as a back-end starter with middling peripherals. Neither pitcher provides a significant platoon advantage or park factor edge at American Family Field. When the model returns a 50% probability, it's signaling that observable skill differentials are minimal. We're in pure variance territory.

## The 50% Projection Dilemma

Here's the sabermetric truth: a 50% pick is simultaneously our most honest projection and our least useful recommendation. There's no expected value edge. No Kelly Criterion would suggest a bet. Yet for tracking purposes, we log it as Milwaukee based on home field's marginal historical value. Consider this pick a placeholder for "these teams are statistically indistinguishable today."

## Expected Value Framework

With yesterday's 55% pick converting and today's projection sitting at the median, we're seeing the model operate across its full probability spectrum. The key metric isn't whether we go 2-0—it's whether our projected probabilities calibrate correctly over time. A properly calibrated model should see 50% picks win exactly half the time, 60% picks win 60% of the time, and so forth. Two games gives us nothing. Two hundred games gives us calibration curves.

Stay sharp. Trust the process. Respect the variance.
